case_study_insert.main_stem: Meridian Leisure Group (MLG) is a partnership in the leisure sector, running an indoor theme park and family attractions in a large city. Founded in 2003 by Elena Vasquez, it employs a workforce of 200 and operates a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership. MLG plans to invest $750,000 in a new indoor leisure dome with automated ride-monitoring and contactless ticketing, financed by a $500,000 ten-year bank loan and $250,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $720,000 a year, a variable cost of $28 a unit and a selling price of $88, and currently produces 40,000 units a year. MLG faces rising labour turnover among ride operators and increasing visitor complaints about queue times.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations and Quality Report — Q4 2026: MLG sold 40,000 admissions (units) last year, up from 36,500 a year ago. Ride inspection found a 3.4% defect rate, down from 5.9% previously. Visitor complaints fell from 58 to 31 per month, and average queue time is 24 minutes. A survey of 700 visitors found that 63% would pay a $12 premium for fast-track entry and 49% book online. A bonus scheme for ride operators is being piloted; on-the-job training covers routine rides while off-the-job training on automated ride-monitoring at the technical college costs $540 per employee, and 22 of the 200 staff need it.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Meridian Leisure Group as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.75% to 5.5%, raising borrowing costs for variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage rises by 6.4% from $13.60 to $14.47 per hour from May 2026, lifting wage bills across leisure. (3) Energy and maintenance input costs have risen 12.3% year-on-year, while consumer spending on leisure attractions grew 4.8% in the same period.

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages for MLG of using a ten-year bank loan rather than an overdraft to fund the $750,000 leisure-dome expansion.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A ten-year bank loan gives MLG a fixed repayment schedule matched to the long life of the $750,000 indoor dome, whereas an overdraft is repayable on demand and could be withdrawn just as the $500,000 is needed. With $720,000 of fixed costs a year, predictable instalments make budgeting far easier, especially as the base rate has risen from 4.75% to 5.5%.

Point 2: The loan provides a large, committed $500,000 alongside $250,000 retained profit, so MLG can complete the automated ride-monitoring project without draining the cash needed to run 40,000 admissions and ease the 24-minute queue time. An overdraft would leave the partnership exposed to sudden calls on its cash and could undermine the 3.4% defect-rate improvements just as the new dome opens.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to MLG's financing decision.

questions.question_text: Consider city-wide billboard advertising, local radio sponsorship, or social media influencer marketing. Which should MLG choose to promote its new indoor leisure dome? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
City-wide billboard advertising: Large billboards would create high visibility for the new dome across the city and support a premium family brand. However, production and site rentals are costly against $720,000 of fixed costs, the message cannot show the automated ride-monitoring, and exposure cannot be measured or tied to the 49% of surveyed visitors who book online.

Social media influencer marketing: Family influencers can film the rides and fast-track entry, reaching exactly the visitors in appendix 1 — the 63% of 700 surveyed visitors who would pay a $12 premium. Engagement is measurable and cheap per view, but much of the audience may live outside the city catchment, and a youth-focused following may convert poorly into the 40,000 admissions needed to fill the dome.

Local radio sponsorship: Local radio is inexpensive, reaches listeners in MLG's immediate city catchment and suits urgent messages about opening days and shorter queues. It can drive same-day visits, which matters because the partnership faces 24-minute queue times and 58-to-31 monthly complaints. Its limits are a narrow geographic reach and no visual demonstration of the dome's features.

Recommendation: MLG should choose local radio sponsorship. It targets the city audience that can actually visit, is affordable beside the $750,000 project, and can promote quick-entry messages that address the queue complaint. Billboards are rejected as expensive and unmeasurable, and influencers are rejected as too geographically diffuse to guarantee 40,000 admissions; MLG should reinforce radio with in-park signage and its online booking channel.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the promotional options with minimal application to MLG.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of MLG with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of MLG with a well-justified recommendation explaining why billboards and influencers are rejected.

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits for MLG of using a bonus scheme to improve motivation among its ride operators.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A bonus tied to smooth, safe operations gives MLG's 200 employees a direct financial reward for keeping rides running and queues moving, which raises effort and helps reduce the rising labour turnover among ride operators. Operators who benefit when the park handles 40,000 admissions are more likely to stay, cutting the disruption that feeds the 58-to-31 visitor-complaint fall.

Point 2: Bonuses focus staff on measurable outcomes such as the 3.4% ride-inspection defect rate and the 24-minute average queue, so the incentive supports the $750,000 dome's automated ride-monitoring rather than working against it. Retaining experienced operators also saves part of the $540 per employee certification cost for the 22 of the 200 staff who need it, protecting capacity in the hierarchical structure.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to MLG's turnover, defects and admissions.

questions.question_text: MLG must upskill 22 of its 200 staff on the new automated ride-monitoring system. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the technical college. Which should MLG choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Senior operators can teach the 22 staff on MLG's own rides and contactless ticketing, so the skills match the exact equipment, cost no fees and keep all 22 available during the busy launch of the $750,000 dome. Coaching can be built into shifts, protecting the 40,000 admissions and the effort to cut the 24-minute queue. The weakness is that trainers pass on their own habits, and without certification the 3.4% defect-rate gains are hard to verify.

Off-the-job training: The technical college course at $540 per employee, $11,880 for 22 people, gives structured teaching and a recognised certificate, a small sum beside the $750,000 investment. It takes 22 of 200 staff off the rides during the launch, however, which could lengthen queues and undermine the 58-to-31 complaint improvement, and generic content would need site familiarisation afterwards.

Decision: MLG should choose on-the-job training delivered by senior operators, with a short certified college module afterwards for lead technicians. This keeps capacity high while labour turnover is a problem and is directly relevant to the ride-monitoring system. Full off-the-job training is rejected because removing 22 staff at launch would worsen the 24-minute queue and the $540 fees can be spent later on formal certification.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to MLG.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of the training methods in the context of MLG.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods in the context of MLG with a well-justified decision covering cost, disruption and equipment relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how MLG's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $720,000 ÷ ($88 − $28) = $720,000 ÷ $60 = 12,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 12,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $88 − $28 = $60. Answer: contribution per unit is $60.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways MLG's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Break-even and margin of safety: 40,000 admissions against a 12,000-unit break-even leaves 28,000 units of buffer, showing how far visitor numbers could fall before the park loses money.
2. Pricing: at $88 an admission the $60 contribution covers the $720,000 fixed costs after 12,000 units, so any fast-track discount must keep contribution positive.
3. Financing: the $60 contribution indicates the extra admissions needed to service the $500,000 bank loan and earn a return on the $750,000 dome.
4. Cost benchmarking: average total cost is $46 ($720,000 ÷ 40,000 + $28), and labour productivity is 40,000 ÷ 200 = 200 units per employee, giving a baseline for judging the 3.4% defect rate and the 24-minute queue time.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 12,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $60 | (iii) Four contextual uses: margin of safety of 28,000 units against 40,000 admissions; pricing control at $88 with $60 contribution; servicing the $500,000 loan and $750,000 dome; and benchmarking at $46 a unit with labour productivity of 200 units per employee to tackle the 3.4% defect rate and 24-minute queue.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate MLG's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has MLG's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.00 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.20 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.75 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.93 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $55,000 inventories + $95,000 trade receivables + $70,000 cash = $220,000; against $220,000 of short-term obligations this gives 1.00, and without inventories $165,000 ÷ $220,000 = 0.75. In 2025 current assets = $60,000 + $120,000 + $95,000 = $275,000 against $230,000 owed, giving 1.20; excluding stock, $215,000 ÷ $230,000 = 0.93.

Evaluation: Short-term liquidity improved. The broad measure rose from exactly 1.00 to 1.20 as cash grew from $70,000 to $95,000 and receivables from $95,000 to $120,000, while current liabilities rose only from $220,000 to $230,000. The stricter measure, which strips out inventories, improved from 0.75 to 0.93 but is still below 1, so MLG continues to rely on stock to meet near-term debts — important while it services a $500,000 loan and builds the $750,000 dome. Receivables grew by $25,000, tying up cash; if corporate customers pay late, the gain could erode quickly.

Conclusion: MLG's financial position has improved, since both measures are higher and the rise is led by cash rather than stock. However, the stricter measure remains under 1, so managers should tighten credit control before treating the $750,000 expansion as fully funded from a strong liquidity base.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of inventories, receivables and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether MLG's financial position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for MLG of offering fast-track entry at a $12 premium.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: The $12 premium follows appendix 1, where 63% of 700 surveyed visitors would pay more for fast-track entry and 49% already book online. It raises revenue above the $88 base admission and protects the $60 contribution per unit as energy and maintenance costs rise 12.3% and the 6.4% wage increase takes effect, helping MLG recover the $750,000 spent on the indoor dome.

Disadvantage: Fast-track lanes may require extra staff and separate queuing space, pushing up the $28 variable cost per unit and the $720,000 fixed costs, so margins narrow if fewer than the surveyed 63% buy the upgrade. Ordinary-queue visitors may feel disadvantaged, which could lift the 58-to-31 monthly complaints and worsen the 24-minute average queue perception just as the new dome opens.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to MLG's research data, costs and expansion.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the rise in the base interest rate to 5.5%, the 6.4% minimum wage increase and the 12.3% rise in input costs will affect MLG. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Base interest rate rise from 4.75% to 5.5%: If MLG's $500,000 ten-year bank loan is variable-rate, the 0.75-point rise adds 0.75% × $500,000 = $3,750 a year (0.0075 × $500,000). That is small compared with $720,000 of fixed costs, and if the loan is fixed-rate the extra cost is zero. Higher rates may still trim family spending on leisure, although spending on attractions grew 4.8%, and MLG can limit the risk by fixing the rate.

Minimum wage rise of 6.4% from $13.60 to $14.47 per hour: With a workforce of 200 this feeds into the wage bill and cannot be avoided. The insert states neither hours worked nor individual pay, so no annual total can be calculated honestly. The defensible comparison is productivity: 40,000 units ÷ 200 staff = 200 units per employee, so the rise is affordable only if productivity holds or admissions grow; otherwise unit labour cost rises and the $60 contribution shrinks.

Input-cost inflation of 12.3%: The insert does not decompose the $28 variable cost, so only an upper bound can be shown: if all $28 were exposed, 12.3% × $28 = $3.444 a unit, and at 40,000 admissions that is $137,760 a year. A smaller exposed share would cost proportionally less. MLG can recover part through the $12 fast-track premium that 63% of 700 surveyed visitors said they would pay.

Conclusion: The 12.3% input-cost inflation has the greatest impact. It is charged across all 40,000 admissions and directly erodes the $60 contribution that supports the $750,000 dome, whereas the interest effect is only $3,750 and the wage effect depends on unknown hours. MLG should negotiate fixed-price energy deals and promote the $12 premium.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to MLG.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on MLG's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of MLG with a well-justified judgement that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the others are smaller.
